summary.oneLiner: Balrampur Chini navigated a 7.5% cane cost hike in FY26 via operational efficiency and volume growth, while positioning its first-of-its-kind PLA plant for imminent commercial ramp-up amid rising fossil plastic prices. The core thesis hinges on the transition from sugar cyclicality to high-margin bioplastics, supported by lowest-in-memory sugar inventory levels and anticipated government ethanol price corrections.
summary.business: Founded in 1975 and headquartered in Kolkata, the Company manufactures sugar, produces ethanol and industrial alcohol from its distilleries, and co-generates bagasse-based power, operating as a fully integrated agri-processing enterprise. Sugar is sold domestically to authorised agents and institutional buyers through an extensive broker network, with export volumes routed via merchant exporters; ethanol is supplied to public and private Oil Marketing Companies; and co-generated power is supplied to distribution companies through the UPPCL state grid and under Open Access. The Company describes its expanding non-sugar revenue streams as strengthening earnings resilience and reducing exposure to sugar-cycle volatility, and is implementing a forward-integration foray into polylactic acid (PLA), which has been identified as a separate reportable segment.

Distillery: Ethanol (green fuel for blending with petrol)
Cogeneration: Co-generated bagasse-based green power (NIC 35106), majorly for captive use
Agro products: Agro-based products sold directly to farmers and to institutional buyers
Polylactic acid (under implementation): Poly lactic acid, a bio-based plastic alternative

endMarkets: Domestic sugar market - authorised agents and institutional buyers reached through an extensive network of brokers|Oil Marketing Companies, public and private, for ethanol supplied under the petrol blending programme|Institutional buyers of industrial alcohol for various industrial applications|State electricity distribution companies via the UPPCL grid and under the Open Access system for co-generated power|Farmers and institutional buyers for agro products|19 States and Union Territories nationally; exports were H36.57 crore or 0.58% of revenue from operations, routed primarily through merchant exporters, with part of the current year's sugar exported to Nepal

currentContext.strengths: Fully integrated business model spanning sugar, ethanol and cogeneration, which the Company says enables revenue diversification and margin cushioning and has reduced exposure to cyclicality in the sugar market|Scale: the Company states it possesses the second largest sugar manufacturing capacity in India, with ten plants concentrated in the cane-abundant regions of eastern and central Uttar Pradesh, forming one of the industry's most integrated capacities|Among the largest distillery operators within the Uttar Pradesh sugar sector, with 1,050 KLPD across five distilleries|Strong credit profile: a long-term rating of AA+ with stable outlook and a short-term rating of A1+ reaffirmed by CRISIL, with India Ratings re-affirming Ind AA+ (Stable) and Ind A1+|Experienced and stable workforce - 5,985 employees as on 31st March 2026, of whom about 80% have worked with the Company for five years or longer, spanning agriculture, IT, finance, manufacturing and ESG functions|Strong rural linkage in established catchment areas supporting assured cane availability, reinforced by supplying farmers with superior seed varieties to raise yields|Stated track record of capital returns: six share buybacks over a ten-year period with a total outlay of H1,009.49 crore (including H110.73 crore in taxes), complemented by cumulative dividend payouts of H655.20 crore (inclusive of H52.46 crore of dividend distribution tax)|Zero liquid discharge incinerator systems installed across distillery operations, which the Company says allowed production to be extended by nearly 60 additional days each year, subject to feedstock availability|Sustained investment in modern manufacturing technology and backend IT infrastructure aimed at efficiency and sustainability|External recognition for energy conservation, cogeneration, CSR and ESG reporting, including the National Energy Conservation Award 2025 for the Babhnan unit and the National Cogeneration Award (Rank I) for the Akbarpur plant
currentContext.strategies: Forward integration and diversification into polylactic acid (PLA): the PLA project announced in February 2024 is under implementation with a revised capital outlay of H3,08,000 lakhs, funded through a mix of equity (a proposed preferential issue), internal accruals and debt.|Elevate PLA to a core business line - given the significance of the emerging business and its prospects, PLA has been identified as a separate reportable segment.|Prioritise the PLA capital programme over incremental cash returns: citing the PLA outlay, the Board confirmed the interim dividend already declared and paid as the final dividend for the year.|Shift distillery feedstock towards grain (maize) and B-heavy molasses alongside the syrup route - grain-based ethanol production rose sharply in FY 25-26, driving higher overall industrial alcohol output.|Advocate, at industry and policy level, for reinstatement of a formula-based ethanol pricing mechanism that compensates for the sugar sacrificed, with management stating that any further ethanol demand or lifting should come only after an upward revision in ethanol prices.|Stay a standalone operating company rather than a group structure - the Company has no subsidiaries or joint ventures and holds a single associate, Auxilo Finserve Private Limited.|Retain employee alignment through the BCML Employees Stock Appreciation Rights Plan 2023, under which equity shares were allotted during the year.
currentContext.expansion: The dominant expansion story is the Polylactic Acid (PLA) project, announced in February 2024 and under implementation through FY 25-26. The Company describes it as a forward-integration/diversification move into a bio-based plastic alternative, carrying a revised capital outlay of H3,08,000 lakhs to be funded through a mix of equity (a proposed preferential issue), internal accruals and debt. The corporate overview lists one poly lactic acid unit of 250 TPD as under implementation; the notes on capital commitments describe the ongoing PLA project as having a capacity of 80,000 tonnes per annum (TPA), with commitments comprising contracts entered into with domestic and overseas vendors for the supply of plant and equipment and core items. Because part of these capital commitments are foreign-currency denominated, the Company has entered into foreign exchange forward contracts, measured at fair value at each balance sheet date. The project is already visible in the balance-sheet discussion: MD&A attributes the 18.23% rise in capital employed and the 58.16% rise in net fixed assets to the ongoing PLA project, notes fresh borrowings of H508.00 crore raised for it, and states that interest on term loans borrowed for the PLA project was capitalised. Beyond PLA, the AR frames expansion historically rather than prospectively: the capacity base of 80,000 TCD of crushing, 1,050 KLPD of distillery and 175.7 MW of saleable cogeneration was built through five decades of acquisitions (Babhnan 1990, Tulsipur 1995, Rauzagaon from Dhampur Sugar Mills, and the Maizapur sugar division carved out of Indo Gulf Industries), greenfield complexes (Haidergarh, Akbarpur, Mankapur, Kumbhi, Gularia) and successive debottlenecking of existing units. The most recent capacity additions described are the 160 KLPD distillery at Gularia (later scaled to 200 KLPD) and the fifth distillery at Maizapur with an installed capacity of 320 KLPD, which together the Company says position it among the largest distillery operators in the Uttar Pradesh sugar sector. The Company also installed incinerator systems across its distillery operations to achieve zero liquid discharge, which it says extended production by nearly 60 additional days each year subject to feedstock availability. No new sugar-mill, cogeneration or distillery expansion project with a stated timeline is disclosed in this bundle beyond PLA.
currentContext.mdna: Indian sugar supply is loosening modestly: net sugar production for SS 25-26 is estimated at ~28.0 MMT versus 26.1 MMT the previous season, with gross output before diversion at ~31.0 MMT versus 29.5 MMT, an increase of about 1.5 MMT or ~6%.|Sugar diverted to ethanol in SS 2025-26 is estimated at ~3 MMT against ~3.4 MMT in the previous season - a lower diversion that management links directly to the absence of ethanol price revisions.|Domestic sugar demand is expected at ~28 MMT versus 28.10 MMT the previous season, with India's carry-forward stock as on 30th September 2026 expected at ~4.30 MMT, implying a tighter closing position.|Exports are a limited lever: the government permitted 1.58 MMT of exports for SS 2025-26, but only ~0.70 MMT is expected to be shipped given the ongoing West Asia crisis, trade disruption, higher freight costs and unfavourable global price parity; sugar exports have additionally been placed on the restrictive list until 30.09.2026.|Cane cost is rising ahead of realisations: the FRP for sugar season 2026-27 has been raised to H365 per quintal, an increase of H10 per quintal, after a ~16.4% rise from H305 to H355 per quintal over recent seasons.|Ethanol economics are the central margin question - no increase in juice/B-heavy route ethanol prices was announced for ethanol years 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 despite the FRP increases, and management notes the sugar sector's share of ethanol supply to OMCs has fallen sharply every year as a result.|The sugar MSP has not been raised from H31 per kg since 2019 despite higher cane FRP and other input costs, compressing the spread available to millers.|Distillery volumes are the growth engine: industrial alcohol production rose to 2,700.10 lakh BL from 2,176.69 lakh BL, driven by higher feedstock availability under the grain and B-heavy molasses routes, with grain (maize) ethanol at 474.56 lakh BL versus 173.06 lakh BL and B-heavy route ethanol at 965.65 lakh BL versus 719.97 lakh BL.|Syrup-route ethanol realisation was flat at an average H65.61 per BL, unchanged from the prior year, with volumes slightly lower.|Cane crushing was essentially flat at 1,031.55 lakh quintals versus 1,033.99 lakh quintals, a 0.24% decline attributed to lower crushing in Q1FY26 compared with Q1FY25.|The agro/bio-products line (mainly Potash derived from Molasses, sold to farmers and to IFFCO) is small and declined year on year.|Global sugar is expected to stay broadly balanced in FY 2026 with production of ~181-189 MMT in 2025-26, improving availability and rebuilding inventories, which management says could cap sustained upward movement in international prices; Brazil remains the dominant exporter and India's policy stance a key swing factor.|Macro backdrop is supportive but externally exposed - India grew an estimated 7.7% in FY 25-26 with CPI inflation around 2.1% and a 125 bps cumulative repo rate cut since February 2025, while the rupee depreciated around 10% against the dollar and the escalation of the US-Iran conflict in early 2026 raised crude and shipping-route volatility.|Management frames the policy prize explicitly: by reverting to proven pricing mechanisms, government could transform the sugar sector from a cyclical, subsidy-dependent industry into a self-sustaining energy powerhouse.

risks.risk: Cane availability - the single largest input risk, driven by area under cane, farmer crop economics, weather and leakage of cane to competing buyers
risks.note: The Company's own risk-mitigation table treats cane availability as the lead strategic and business risk. Area under cane falls when alternate crops such as wheat, mustard, paddy and maize fetch higher revenue on MSP increases, or when cane yields drop. Yield is hit by untimely or short, heavy rainfall, high summer temperatures, and high incidence of insects, pests and diseases; supply is further lost to diversion of cane to nearby mills and to kohlu and crushers that sometimes pay above SAP, and to damage by stray animals. Mitigation is relationship-led and structurally slow to change - timely payment and procurement, village and factory meetings, technical help, irrigation guidance, flood-tolerant varieties such as CoLK 94184, desilting of water bodies, wire-net fencing and Jhatka machines, expanded Gaushalas, and indent and transport management. BRSR separately lists Supply Chain Management as a material risk on the same grounds, adding variation in cane quality parameters such as sucrose content and extraneous matter as a hit to production efficiency and product quality.

risks.risk: Sugar recovery and varietal concentration - the collapse of the high-sugar Co 0238 variety to red rot with no matching replacement
risks.note: Recovery depends mainly on varietal balance, and the area under the high-sugared Co 0238 variety has reduced because of red rot incidence, with the Company stating that no matching variety with sizeable area is available to date. The fallback set is imperfect: older Co 118 recovery is only at par with Co 0238; new Co 15023 has better recovery but is still at the adoption stage with area rising only gradually; CoLK 14201 is good but needs timely planting. More than 50 new varieties are under trial with five shortlisted for closer review before commercial planting, so replacement is a multi-season process. Because recovery drives both sugar output and the cane cost per tonne of sugar, this is a durable margin risk, not a one-year event.

risks.risk: Ethanol price stagnation decoupled from cane cost - the input price is administered upward while the output price is frozen
risks.note: No increase in ethanol prices was announced for the juice/B-heavy route for ethanol years 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 despite the cane FRP rising about 16.4% from H305 to H355 per quintal, with the FRP for 2026-27 raised again to H365. Management states the shift from a predictable, formula-based pricing model to the current stagnation has essentially decoupled the output price (ethanol) from the input cost (sugarcane FRP), threatening the stability of the entire ecosystem, and notes the sugar sector's share of ethanol supply to OMCs has fallen drastically every year as a result. This directly compresses the economics of the distillery segment, which is the Company's principal non-sugar earnings stream, and the required remedy sits with government rather than with the Company.

risks.risk: Pervasive government policy dependence across pricing, exports and diversion
risks.note: Profitability is set as much by administrative decisions as by operations - cane FRP and the Uttar Pradesh State Advised Price, ethanol procurement prices, the sugar minimum selling price and monthly sale quotas, stock-holding limits, and export permissions. Export volumes are effectively rationed: the government permitted 1.58 MMT for SS 2025-26 but only about 0.70 MMT is expected to ship. The MD&A's own sector SWOT names high regulatory dependence, policy volatility including export bans, stock limits or diversion caps, and a sector long shaped by political agendas. The Company can hedge operationally but cannot control the price of either its main input or a major output.

risks.risk: Structural cyclicality and working-capital intensity of a single-crop, single-state footprint
risks.note: All ten manufacturing units sit in eastern and central Uttar Pradesh and depend on one crop, so a regional monsoon failure, pest outbreak or state-level pricing decision hits the entire asset base at once. The sector SWOT identifies a cyclical earnings profile driven by production surplus and deficit cycles and working-capital-intensive operations, especially during peak crushing seasons. The Company's stated risk philosophy is framed around exactly this - the central aim in the sugar industry is to stabilise operational and commercial factors as far as practicable, reducing exposure to volatility.

risks.risk: Execution and funding risk on the Polylactic Acid project, a new business outside the Company's operating history
risks.note: The PLA project carries a revised capital outlay of H3,08,000 lakhs funded through a mix of equity (a proposed preferential issue), internal accruals and debt, and the Board withheld a separate final dividend in view of that outlay. It is the Company's first move into bio-based polymers, with plant and equipment contracted from domestic and overseas vendors and foreign-currency exposure hedged through forward contracts. The Risk Management Committee explicitly names identifying and proactively managing risks associated with new business initiatives as one of its defined action areas, which is where this exposure is governed.

risks.risk: Occupational health and safety in high-temperature, chemical and heavy-machinery operations
risks.note: Identified as a material BRSR issue with negative financial implications. Operations involving high temperatures, chemicals and heavy machinery expose workers to occupational hazards, raising the risk of workplace accidents, injuries and operational disruptions, while extended working hours in high-temperature environments and physical strain from manual handling may adversely affect employee health and well-being. Mitigation runs through site-specific safety protocols, emergency response drills, certified PPE, preventive maintenance, regular health check-ups and safety training, with HIRA protocols and continual improvement of the ISO 45001 management system framed as the upside case.

risks.risk: Product quality, food safety and the customer confidence that depends on them
risks.note: Identified as material BRSR risks with negative financial implications. Non-compliance with quality standards can trigger regulatory action and reputational damage affecting consumer trust and brand credibility, while improper storage, handling or transportation of finished product can cause deterioration. Failure to meet customer expectations on quality, timely delivery or service can impair customer confidence and business relationships - a live concern given that sugar is sold to authorised agents and institutional buyers through brokers and ethanol to OMCs, so a small number of counterparties carry large volumes. Mitigation runs through quality management systems aligned to FSSAI requirements and FSSC 22000, farm-to-factory traceability, warehouse condition monitoring, and timely grievance redressal.

one-line thesis: Balrampur Chini navigated a 7.5% cane cost hike in FY26 via operational efficiency and volume growth, while positioning its first-of-its-kind PLA plant for imminent commercial ramp-up amid rising fossil plastic prices. The core thesis hinges on the transition from sugar cyclicality to high-margin bioplastics, supported by lowest-in-memory sugar inventory levels and anticipated government ethanol price corrections.
financial scorecard: Revenue: Stable growth driven by 5.2% higher cane crushing (1,043 lakh quintals) offsetting margin pressure; EBITDA/Margin: Sugar segment resilient despite SAP hike from INR 370 to 400/quintal, Ethanol margins compressed due to 3-year price freeze; PAT: Not explicitly quantified in transcript but implied stable due to volume mix; Order Book: PLA inquiries advanced but no formal offtake announced yet; Net Debt: Funding INR 3,080 crore capex via INR 450 crore preferential issue (promoters contributed INR 193 crore) to limit dilution.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Linked to PLA commissioning in Q3FY27 and potential ethanol price revision; Margin: Targeting 35% EBITDA on PLA (excluding incentives); Order Inflow: PLA customer finalization nearing completion; Capex/Commissioning: PLA plant commissioning expected Oct 2026 (Q3), Lacto-gypsum plant approved at Kumbhi.
order book & pipeline: PLA commercial agreements in advanced stages with multiple customers awaiting production commitment; no specific tonnage disclosed but 'progressing well' with testing complete for barrier properties.
segment / subsidiary detail: Sugar: Crushed 1,043 lakh quintals (+5.2% YoY), recovery 11.24% (vs 11.28%); Ethanol: Produced 27 crore liters in FY26, capacity expandable to 34-35 crore liters, shift towards B-heavy/Juice route due to volume constraints in C-heavy; PLA: First integrated plant in India, leveraging captive sugar/bagasse for cost advantage.
growth verticals / optionality: Expansion of PLA capacity with 15-18 month execution timeline post-decision; E85/E100 ethanol blending roadmap driving future demand; Gypsum board manufacturing from PLA by-products.
margins & cost dynamics: PLA margins protected by zero logistics cost on sugar/bagasse and captive power vs peers; Sugar margins pressured by INR 30/quintal SAP hike; Ethanol margins stagnant due to lack of price revision since FY23.
capex / expansion: Total revised capex INR 3,080 crore for PLA integration; INR 450 crore raised via preferential shares; Lacto-gypsum plant additional investment.
capital allocation: Preferential equity raise to fund capex without promoter dilution (proportionate participation); Focus on integrated value chain over M&A.
risks & watch-items: Delay in government ethanol price revision; Uncertainty on non-plastic mandate timeline (expected sooner than 6 months but not guaranteed); Crop yield dependency on monsoon (assessment possible only by Aug-Sept); PLA market adoption speed vs fossil plastic price volatility.
management quality / tone: Confident on PLA technical readiness and cost advantages; Cautiously optimistic on ethanol pricing ('fingers crossed'); Transparent on sugar recovery challenges (0238 variety replacement difficult).
non-obvious takeaways: PLA biodegradation in Indian landfill conditions occurs within one season even if mixed with other materials; Competitors can replicate feedstock advantages but lack Balrampur's 2-year R&D headstart; Customers waiting for production commitment before switching suppliers despite validated quality.

hero.oneLiner: Balrampur Chini navigated a 7.5% cane cost hike in FY26 via operational efficiency and volume growth, while positioning its first-of-its-kind PLA plant for imminent commercial ramp-up amid rising fossil plastic prices. The core thesis hinges on the transition from sugar cyclicality to high-margin bioplastics, supported by lowest-in-memory sugar inventory levels and anticipated government ethanol price corrections.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Founded in 1975 and headquartered in Kolkata, the Company manufactures sugar, produces ethanol and industrial alcohol from its distilleries, and co-generates bagasse-based power, operating as a fully integrated agri-processing enterprise. Sugar is sold domestically to authorised agents and institutional buyers through an extensive broker network, with export volumes routed via merchant exporters; ethanol is supplied to public and private Oil Marketing Companies; and co-generated power is supplied to distribution companies through the UPPCL state grid and under Open Access. The Company describes its expanding non-sugar revenue streams as strengthening earnings resilience and reducing exposure to sugar-cycle volatility, and is implementing a forward-integration foray into polylactic acid (PLA), which has been identified as a separate reportable segment.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian sugar supply is loosening modestly: net sugar production for SS 25-26 is estimated at ~28.0 MMT versus 26.1 MMT the previous season, with gross output before diversion at ~31.0 MMT versus 29.5 MMT, an increase of about 1.5 MMT or ~6%.
- Sugar diverted to ethanol in SS 2025-26 is estimated at ~3 MMT against ~3.4 MMT in the previous season - a lower diversion that management links directly to the absence of ethanol price revisions.
- Domestic sugar demand is expected at ~28 MMT versus 28.10 MMT the previous season, with India's carry-forward stock as on 30th September 2026 expected at ~4.30 MMT, implying a tighter closing position.
- Exports are a limited lever: the government permitted 1.58 MMT of exports for SS 2025-26, but only ~0.70 MMT is expected to be shipped given the ongoing West Asia crisis, trade disruption, higher freight costs and unfavourable global price parity; sugar exports have additionally been placed on the restrictive list until 30.09.2026.
- Cane cost is rising ahead of realisations: the FRP for sugar season 2026-27 has been raised to H365 per quintal, an increase of H10 per quintal, after a ~16.4% rise from H305 to H355 per quintal over recent seasons.
- Ethanol economics are the central margin question - no increase in juice/B-heavy route ethanol prices was announced for ethanol years 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 despite the FRP increases, and management notes the sugar sector's share of ethanol supply to OMCs has fallen sharply every year as a result.
- The sugar MSP has not been raised from H31 per kg since 2019 despite higher cane FRP and other input costs, compressing the spread available to millers.
- Distillery volumes are the growth engine: industrial alcohol production rose to 2,700.10 lakh BL from 2,176.69 lakh BL, driven by higher feedstock availability under the grain and B-heavy molasses routes, with grain (maize) ethanol at 474.56 lakh BL versus 173.06 lakh BL and B-heavy route ethanol at 965.65 lakh BL versus 719.97 lakh BL.
- Syrup-route ethanol realisation was flat at an average H65.61 per BL, unchanged from the prior year, with volumes slightly lower.
- Cane crushing was essentially flat at 1,031.55 lakh quintals versus 1,033.99 lakh quintals, a 0.24% decline attributed to lower crushing in Q1FY26 compared with Q1FY25.
- The agro/bio-products line (mainly Potash derived from Molasses, sold to farmers and to IFFCO) is small and declined year on year.
- Global sugar is expected to stay broadly balanced in FY 2026 with production of ~181-189 MMT in 2025-26, improving availability and rebuilding inventories, which management says could cap sustained upward movement in international prices; Brazil remains the dominant exporter and India's policy stance a key swing factor.
- Macro backdrop is supportive but externally exposed - India grew an estimated 7.7% in FY 25-26 with CPI inflation around 2.1% and a 125 bps cumulative repo rate cut since February 2025, while the rupee depreciated around 10% against the dollar and the escalation of the US-Iran conflict in early 2026 raised crude and shipping-route volatility.
- Management frames the policy prize explicitly: by reverting to proven pricing mechanisms, government could transform the sugar sector from a cyclical, subsidy-dependent industry into a self-sustaining energy powerhouse.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The dominant expansion story is the Polylactic Acid (PLA) project, announced in February 2024 and under implementation through FY 25-26. The Company describes it as a forward-integration/diversification move into a bio-based plastic alternative, carrying a revised capital outlay of H3,08,000 lakhs to be funded through a mix of equity (a proposed preferential issue), internal accruals and debt. The corporate overview lists one poly lactic acid unit of 250 TPD as under implementation; the notes on capital commitments describe the ongoing PLA project as having a capacity of 80,000 tonnes per annum (TPA), with commitments comprising contracts entered into with domestic and overseas vendors for the supply of plant and equipment and core items. Because part of these capital commitments are foreign-currency denominated, the Company has entered into foreign exchange forward contracts, measured at fair value at each balance sheet date. The project is already visible in the balance-sheet discussion: MD&A attributes the 18.23% rise in capital employed and the 58.16% rise in net fixed assets to the ongoing PLA project, notes fresh borrowings of H508.00 crore raised for it, and states that interest on term loans borrowed for the PLA project was capitalised. Beyond PLA, the AR frames expansion historically rather than prospectively: the capacity base of 80,000 TCD of crushing, 1,050 KLPD of distillery and 175.7 MW of saleable cogeneration was built through five decades of acquisitions (Babhnan 1990, Tulsipur 1995, Rauzagaon from Dhampur Sugar Mills, and the Maizapur sugar division carved out of Indo Gulf Industries), greenfield complexes (Haidergarh, Akbarpur, Mankapur, Kumbhi, Gularia) and successive debottlenecking of existing units. The most recent capacity additions described are the 160 KLPD distillery at Gularia (later scaled to 200 KLPD) and the fifth distillery at Maizapur with an installed capacity of 320 KLPD, which together the Company says position it among the largest distillery operators in the Uttar Pradesh sugar sector. The Company also installed incinerator systems across its distillery operations to achieve zero liquid discharge, which it says extended production by nearly 60 additional days each year subject to feedstock availability. No new sugar-mill, cogeneration or distillery expansion project with a stated timeline is disclosed in this bundle beyond PLA.

management_tone.body: Confident on PLA technical readiness and cost advantages; Cautiously optimistic on ethanol pricing ('fingers crossed'); Transparent on sugar recovery challenges (0238 variety replacement difficult).

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Fully integrated business model spanning sugar, ethanol and cogeneration, which the Company says enables revenue diversification and margin cushioning and has reduced exposure to cyclicality in the sugar market
- Scale: the Company states it possesses the second largest sugar manufacturing capacity in India, with ten plants concentrated in the cane-abundant regions of eastern and central Uttar Pradesh, forming one of the industry's most integrated capacities
- Among the largest distillery operators within the Uttar Pradesh sugar sector, with 1,050 KLPD across five distilleries
- Strong credit profile: a long-term rating of AA+ with stable outlook and a short-term rating of A1+ reaffirmed by CRISIL, with India Ratings re-affirming Ind AA+ (Stable) and Ind A1+
- Experienced and stable workforce - 5,985 employees as on 31st March 2026, of whom about 80% have worked with the Company for five years or longer, spanning agriculture, IT, finance, manufacturing and ESG functions
- Strong rural linkage in established catchment areas supporting assured cane availability, reinforced by supplying farmers with superior seed varieties to raise yields
- Stated track record of capital returns: six share buybacks over a ten-year period with a total outlay of H1,009.49 crore (including H110.73 crore in taxes), complemented by cumulative dividend payouts of H655.20 crore (inclusive of H52.46 crore of dividend distribution tax)
- Zero liquid discharge incinerator systems installed across distillery operations, which the Company says allowed production to be extended by nearly 60 additional days each year, subject to feedstock availability
- Sustained investment in modern manufacturing technology and backend IT infrastructure aimed at efficiency and sustainability
- External recognition for energy conservation, cogeneration, CSR and ESG reporting, including the National Energy Conservation Award 2025 for the Babhnan unit and the National Cogeneration Award (Rank I) for the Akbarpur plant

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [State incentive] Uttar Pradesh's Bio Plastic Industrial Policy 2024 (announced 4th October 2024) gives investors of Rs. 1,000 crore or more a 50% capital subsidy on eligible investment disbursed over 7 years after commercial production, 5% interest subvention for 7 years, 100% SGST (net) reimbursement for 10 years, electricity duty exemption for 10 years and stamp duty exemption; total incentive capped at 200% of eligible investment. Invest UP has issued a Letter of Comfort to the company approving eligibility, subject to commencement of commercial operations and stipulated conditions.
- [Subsidy condition] The capital subsidy is linked to a Gross Capacity Utilisation Multiple (GCM): GCM is 1 if actual production to installed capacity is 40% in the 1st year, and 75% in subsequent years.
- [Ethanol policy] For ESY 2025-26 OMCs have contracted ~1048.4 Cr BL of ethanol; supply till 30th June 2026 was ~717.29 Cr BL, giving blending of ~19.99% (ESY 2024-25: ~1003 Cr BL supplied till 31st October 2025 against ~1131.7 Cr BL contracted, blending ~19.24%). A roadmap for "Beyond E-20" is being worked on by the Government.
- [Feedstock policy] The government has allowed 72 lakh tonnes of FCI rice to be sold at Rs. 23.20 per kg to ethanol distilleries under the EBP programme for ESY 2025-26 - relevant to BCML's newly started rice route.
- [Associate] BCML holds 30.47% of Auxilo Finserve Private Limited (16.53 Cr shares at average cost Rs. 10.59/share, investment Rs. 175.00 crores); Auxilo's net worth as on 30th June 2026 is ~Rs. 1528.37 crores, total assets Rs. 5531 crores, GNPA 0.52%, NNPA 0.12%, CRAR 29.74%, and the value of BCML's investment basis the last equity raise is Rs. 959.40 crores.
